Aiden Clarke gave Stonebridge their first movement, not wildly, not recklessly, just quick enough to stop the new ball from settling into a spell of pure control, while Noah Bell at the other end played the slower and more watchful role, letting the ball come, taking the safer singles, and allowing the innings to breathe through the first pocket of pressure. Dylan Hart broke that opening when Clarke reached once too often and Ryan Wells held the chance, but the wicket did not immediately bring Meadowbrook the squeeze they wanted because Caleb Warren arrived with a more complete tempo than anyone else in the Stonebridge top order. Warren and Bell became the spine of the innings, and their partnership was the passage that Stonebridge later had to look back on as both the source of their total and the missed chance inside it. Bell was not fluent in a spectacular way, yet he stayed, absorbed overs, and gave Warren the stable partner a captain needs when a first innings is trying to turn from decent into heavy. Warren, by contrast, gave the stand its scoring authority. He trusted the bounce earlier, drove straighter when the seamers overpitched, and used the short boundary intelligently enough to make Meadowbrook adjust fields rather than simply bowl to a plan. The stand pushed Stonebridge well past the early uncertainty and into a position where a genuinely large score looked available, but Meadowbrook’s credit lies in how they refused to let that platform become an avalanche. Mason Grey removed Bell just when the partnership had begun to feel permanent, and Ryan Wells then worked his way into the most important phase of his spell, cutting out Ryan Cole before the innings could use the old platform as a springboard. Warren stayed a little longer, but once Wells had him caught by Tyler Grant, the tone of the innings changed. Stonebridge still had batters to come, and Ethan Vale, Dylan Shaw and Lucas Field all found useful touches, but the middle-to-late section never quite became the clean finishing surge the earlier stand had promised. Oliver Reed went early to Evan Turner, and though Tyler Grant’s sharper hand made sure the chase did not freeze, Stonebridge still had enough early energy to believe the target could become uncomfortable if two wickets came close together. Tyler played the best of the early counterpunches, using width well and lifting once cleanly enough to move the field, while Isaac Bennett began the slower work that would later matter more than it looked at first. Connor Blake eventually removed Tyler, and at that point the chase was not in danger but not yet under control either. The real stabilizing passage came through Bennett and Connor Wells. Wells did not bat like a man trying to finish the game in one rush. He played a bridge innings, busy enough to prevent Stonebridge from surrounding Bennett, careful enough not to feed them the cluster they needed. Bennett’s role was even more important because he gave Meadowbrook time. Harper’s innings was the match’s decisive act because it arrived before the chase was safe and ended after the result had already been taken from Stonebridge’s hands. At first he threaded the ball into gaps, testing the field, judging how much risk the chase actually needed. Then, as the required work began to shrink, he became the accelerator Meadowbrook had been waiting for. He hit straight when the bowlers missed full, picked up length into the leg side, and forced Stonebridge to defend two different versions of the chase at once: Bennett’s accumulation and Harper’s force. When Bennett fell, Harper did not let the innings drift into another rebuild. Luke Barrett gave him a short burst of support, Ryan Wells added a small piece, and even when those wickets went, Mason Grey came in with the right temperament for the finish. That last stand mattered because it stopped Stonebridge from turning late wickets into late panic. Grey played clean, uncomplicated cricket, Harper kept the field spread, and the chase moved from calculation to closure. Meadowbrook reached 263 for six in the forty-seventh over, winning by four wickets, and the result felt earned because they had absorbed the one major Stonebridge platform, kept the first innings below the heavier score it threatened, then chased with enough layers to survive every pressure point. Stonebridge had Warren’s controlled captain’s hand, Bell’s long support, Field’s useful finish and a spread of wickets from the bowlers, but they never found the single decisive spell that could split Meadowbrook open. Meadowbrook had that decisive innings instead. Leo Harper’s unbeaten 84 was not only the top score of the chase; it was the performance that changed the emotional shape of the match, turning a target that still needed real work into a pursuit completed with authority, timing and enough wickets left to make the final margin feel fair.

O: Brookfield Oval in Eastmere had that slightly slow feel from the first inspection, the kind of surface where a batting side can build something useful if it accepts hard work, but where fluent scoring never quite arrives for free, so Bayside XI’s decision to bat first made sense on paper and still came with immediate risk once Ridgeway XI began landing the ball into the surface rather than floating it up for easy drives. Ari Cole gave Bayside the first movement of the morning, not in a reckless way, more through controlled boundary strokes whenever Elliot Shaw or Caleb Frost missed wide enough to let him free the hands, while Jonah Miles played the quieter end, leaving more than he scored and trying to make the new ball old enough for the middle order to take over. That opening partnership gave Bayside a workable base, but it never felt dominant because Ridgeway kept the ring tight and made almost every single feel negotiated. Shaw eventually removed Ari just as the start was beginning to look properly useful, and that first wicket changed the tone because Bayside had not raced away, they had only survived into a better position. Caleb Warren then gave the innings its most important shape. He was the one batter who looked capable of turning occupation into control, first alongside Jonah, then more convincingly with Finn Carter, who did not score heavily but stayed long enough to let the captain settle into the rhythm of the pitch. Warren’s innings was not a free-flowing fifty, and that is exactly why it mattered; he had to build it through patience, nudged singles, controlled drives and the occasional heavier shot when Ridgeway overcorrected. The stand with Finn became the best part of Bayside’s innings, though even there the total never took on the feel of a side charging toward something large. Ridgeway’s attack kept making quiet interventions. Ryan Vale removed Finn, Sam Brooks cut off Luca Reed before he could give the middle order a clean bridge, and when Warren himself fell with the score still short of the kind of platform Bayside wanted, the innings began to look more like a collection of useful pieces than one complete statement. Owen Hart and Tyler Cross then gave Bayside their second practical passage, not spectacular, but valuable enough to keep the innings moving through the forties of the over count. Owen did the longer repair work, Tyler added the slightly sharper edge, and for a while Bayside seemed likely to push beyond the low two-hundreds into a more uncomfortable chase. Noah Lane and Sam Brooks made sure that did not happen cleanly. Owen went before the final push could fully form, Tyler followed after a short burst, and Leo Marsh was bowled before the tail could reset. Zane Foster’s not-out hand gave the innings its last bit of punch, and Milo Grant’s small finish mattered because it pushed Bayside to 211 for eight rather than something visibly under par, but Ridgeway walked off knowing they had kept the first innings in reach. The bowling card showed that shared pressure well: Ryan Vale, Brooks and Lane all took pairs of wickets, Shaw and Frost supplied the earlier cuts, and Mason Vale’s few overs were expensive enough to remind everyone that the surface could still be scored from if a batter found his tempo. Chasing 212, Ridgeway needed discipline more than bravado, and Bayside briefly made the target feel trickier than it looked. Oliver Reed was pinned early, Theo Grant countered with enough intent to keep the score moving, but Owen Hart removed him too, leaving Ridgeway two down with the chase still young and enough overs remaining for Bayside to believe a squeeze was possible. That was where Mason Vale began to take ownership of the match. He did not walk in and finish the game in a rush. He first gave the innings shape, then tempo, then authority. Connor Wells helped him through the most important rebuilding passage, playing the captain’s role with restraint, taking time out of the game and preventing Bayside from attacking Mason with an entirely closed field. Their stand was the largest of the chase and the first real shift in Ridgeway’s favour, moving the score from a slightly awkward position into a place where the target started to feel like a calculation rather than a threat. Caleb Warren eventually bowled Wells, which gave Bayside a route back, and when Dylan Stone also fell after helping Mason move the chase through the next phase, the match was still not finished. Ridgeway had wickets in hand but not enough control to be careless. Ryan Wells came and went, Sam Brooks offered a useful late burst, and by the time Lucas Brooks bowled him at 189 for six, Bayside had created the one final moment they needed if the game was going to turn. The issue for them was that Mason Vale was still there. He had already absorbed the early repair work, already handled the middle-overs pressure, and now he read the finish with the calm of a batter who knew exactly how many risks were actually required. Liam Stone joined him and did the simple things correctly, blocking the good ball, taking the run when it was there, and giving Mason the strike often enough for the chase to keep shrinking. Mason’s unbeaten 82 was the innings that joined every part of Ridgeway’s reply together: the rescue after two wickets, the measured rebuild with Wells, the controlled progress with Stone, the response to late wickets, and finally the finishing push. Ridgeway reached 214 for six in the forty-sixth over, winning by four wickets, and the result felt fair because Bayside had enough batting depth to post something competitive but not enough of a defining partnership to make it heavy, while Ridgeway had the one decisive hand in Mason Vale and enough supporting pieces around him to keep the chase from breaking. Bayside’s bowlers shared wickets and kept the match alive longer than the final chase might suggest, but Ridgeway had the clearer match-winner, and in a game where neither innings fully ran away, Mason’s ability to stay, absorb, accelerate and close was the difference.

Marcus Dale and Evan Brooks then produced the one passage of Ridgefield’s innings that looked like a genuine answer rather than a delay. Dale was all restraint, dead hands, little checks into the ground, the kind of opener’s work that does not light up a card but keeps the innings breathing. Brooks was the contrast, much cleaner through the ball, quick to punish anything that sat up, and for a while his strokes changed the sound of the innings. He found the rope often enough to make Harborvale pull the ring back, and their stand, helped here and there by small extras and imperfect lines, carried Ridgefield past the immediate danger and into a position where a more ambitious total was at least imaginable. Caleb Stone broke that bridge at the exact moment Harborvale needed it, Brooks gone after doing almost all the visible scoring in that phase, and from there Ridgefield began to lose the shape they had fought so hard to recover. Marcus Dale stayed a little longer and then went too, Isaac Moore followed without scoring, Tyler Shaw’s stay was more survival than substance, and suddenly the scoreboard had moved from repair into that awkward middle-overs state where every new partnership seems to begin from scratch. Lucas Price gave Ridgefield another useful hand, not a dominant one, but a necessary one, because he was able to turn a few quiet balls into workable overs and helped the lower middle avoid complete collapse. Henry Clarke struck briefly before Daniel Hart cut him off, Ryan Foster tried to add some captain’s resistance, and Blake Turner’s late stay with Aiden Grant dragged the score toward respectability, but none of those pieces fully changed the innings. The pattern kept repeating: one batter looked as if he might hold a passage together, Harborvale found the wicket before the passage became a platform.
